summary: Bromocriptine is an ergot-derived dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin and growth hormone secretion and stimulates dopamine receptors. It treats hyperprolactinemia-associated disorders, prolactinomas, acromegaly and Parkinson disease. Taken with food and titrated slowly to limit nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Key cautions: postpartum use is contraindicated, sudden sleep onset can occur, and it must be withdrawn for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
indications: Hyperprolactinemia-associated dysfunctions: amenorrhea with/without galactorrhea, infertility, hypogonadism
Prolactin-secreting adenomas (including reduction of macroadenoma size, pre-surgical tumor reduction)

dosage.d: Initial 1.25-2.5 mg daily; add 2.5 mg every 2-7 days; usual 2.5-15 mg/day
dosage.n: Use mechanical contraception until ovulatory cycles restored

dosage.d: Initial 1.25-2.5 mg at bedtime x3 days; increase by 1.25-2.5 mg every 3-7 days; usual 20-30 mg/day
Initial 1.25 mg twice daily; increase by 2.5 mg/day every 14-28 days
dosage.n: Titrate slowly; high doses risk hallucinations/dyskinesia

admin: Take with food to reduce the high incidence of nausea/vomiting
Start at the lowest dose, usually with the first dose at bedtime, and titrate slowly
Evaluate frequently during dose escalation to find the lowest effective dose
Perform full pituitary evaluation before treating hyperprolactinemia
Use mechanical contraception in fertility patients until normal ovulatory cycles return
moa: Bromocriptine is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist. By stimulating dopamine receptors on pituitary lactotrophs it inhibits prolactin secretion (treating hyperprolactinemia and shrinking prolactinomas) and lowers growth hormone in acromegaly. In Parkinson disease it directly stimulates striatal postsynaptic dopamine receptors, improving motor function.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to bromocriptine or any ergot alkaloid
Use during the postpartum period in women (especially with coronary artery disease/cardiovascular risk)
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (eclampsia, preeclampsia, pregnancy-induced hypertension) unless withdrawal is contraindicated
relative: History of psychosis or psychiatric disorder
Peptic ulcer disease / GI bleeding history
monitor: Visual fields if macroadenoma during pregnancy

preg: Pregnancy Category B. For hyperprolactinemia, withdraw bromocriptine when pregnancy is diagnosed. If reinstituted for a rapidly expanding macroadenoma and the patient develops a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, weigh continuation against risk. Monitor closely for tumor expansion and visual field changes during pregnancy.
lact: Bromocriptine suppresses lactation and should not be used during the postpartum period or in nursing women. It was associated with serious postpartum cardiovascular events and is contraindicated for postpartum lactation suppression.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is provided in the labeling; use with caution.
hepatic: Bromocriptine undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism (CYP3A4); use caution and consider dose adjustment in hepatic impairment.

major: Other ergot alkaloids - not recommended; additive ergotism/vasospasm
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors) - increase bromocriptine levels
Macrolides (erythromycin) - increase bromocriptine AUC ~3.7-fold and Cmax ~4.6-fold
moderate: Dopamine antagonists (phenothiazines, haloperidol, metoclopramide, pimozide) - decrease bromocriptine efficacy
Octreotide - increases bromocriptine levels (~38%) in acromegaly
minor: Sympathomimetics - hypertension/dysrhythmia risk at high bromocriptine doses
interactions.food: Take with food; food does not significantly change exposure but markedly reduces nausea/vomiting.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may potentiate side effects and cause disulfiram-like intolerance; avoid.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers serum prolactin and growth hormone (therapeutic markers).

monitoring: Blood pressure, especially during initiation and dose escalation (first-dose hypotension)
Visual fields in patients with macroadenoma, particularly during pregnancy
Pregnancy status; cardiopulmonary symptoms with chronic high-dose use
counsel: Take with food and rise slowly to reduce nausea and dizziness
First dose may cause fainting - take at bedtime and have support nearby
Do not drive or operate machinery if you experience drowsiness or sudden sleep episodes
Use a barrier contraceptive until normal cycles return; tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant
Report severe headache, chest pain, visual changes, or unusual urges (gambling/shopping)
pk: Prolactin falls within 1-2 hours of a dose
Elimination half-life ~4.85 hours (effect on prolactin longer)
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); tight, light-resistant container with desiccant
pearls: Contraindicated postpartum - do NOT use for lactation suppression; serious cardiovascular events (HTN, MI, stroke, seizures) reported
Take with food and titrate slowly to manage prominent nausea and first-dose hypotension
Withdraw for any hypertensive disorder of pregnancy unless withdrawal is medically contraindicated
Warn Parkinson patients about sudden sleep onset and impulse control disorders
Erythromycin and azole antifungals markedly raise bromocriptine levels
missed: If a dose is missed, take it with food when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose; then skip it. Do not double up. Take subsequent doses with food to limit nausea.
overdose: Overdose causes nausea, vomiting, dizziness, pallor, severe hypotension, confusion, lethargy, hallucinations and repetitive yawning. The drug has a wide safety margin. Treat with gastric decontamination (emesis if conscious, lavage, activated charcoal), supportive care, fluid balance monitoring, Trendelenburg positioning and IV fluids for hypotension; vasopressors if needed.
